description: 25 AI transformation readiness criteria organized into 5 domains. Each criterion has 3 evidence questions scored 0-3.

criteria.title: AI Operating Rhythm & Decision Rights
criteria.description: The organization connects AI strategy, demand intake, delivery, learning, and governance through a visible operating rhythm with clear decision ownership.
sub_criteria: Is there a documented AI operating rhythm connecting strategy, demand intake, delivery, learning, and governance?
Are decision rights clearly assigned across business, IT, data, architecture, security, legal, and service areas?
Are decisions traceable through meeting cadence, approval records, backlog movement, or escalation logs?

criteria.title: Adaptive AI Demand Routing
criteria.description: AI work is routed through the operating model by work nature, value, uncertainty, risk, capacity, competence, and service ownership instead of using one delivery model for every initiative.
sub_criteria: Are AI demands classified by nature of work: predictable, standardized, iterative, exploratory, or transformative?
Are standardized or predictable AI demands routed through repeatable delivery paths while uncertain or impact-driven AI demands use Launch-and-Learn?
Is demand routing connected to capacity, competence, service-area ownership, value hypothesis, and risk level?

criteria.title: Evidence-Based Launch-and-Learn Model
criteria.description: The organization de-risks AI transformation through Kickstart validation, bounded vertical slices, evidence-based business cases, and explicit conversion into Building-the-System scaling patterns.
sub_criteria: Does the organization start AI transformation from a bounded vertical slice, safe experiment, or Kickstart use case tied to a specific service-area impact statement?
Are pilot learnings captured and used to refine operating model, architecture, data, governance, safety, and value assumptions?
Is there a defined transition from Kickstart validation to Building-the-System scaling, including a pilot playbook or absorption-readiness map?

criteria.title: Shared Learning Architecture
criteria.description: AI knowledge flows through communities, chapters, guilds, and reusable practice rather than remaining isolated in experts or pilot teams.
sub_criteria: Are communities of knowledge, chapters, guilds, or equivalent competence structures used to spread AI learning?
Are lessons from AI pilots, failures, red teaming, and operational incidents converted into reusable practices?
Are business, AI, data, platform, and service teams learning together rather than separately?

criteria.title: Human-AI Work Redesign
criteria.description: AI initiatives redesign work, handoffs, roles, and feedback loops so human capacity moves toward higher-value contribution.
sub_criteria: Are AI initiatives explicitly designed to reallocate human capacity toward higher-value work, not only reduce task time?
Are roles, handoffs, review points, exception paths, and human-in-the-loop responsibilities redesigned?
Are employee experience, cognitive load, quality, and customer impact measured after AI introduction?

criteria.title: Service-Boundary-Based AI Integration
criteria.description: AI systems integrate through reliable service boundaries, brownfield-compatible APIs, events, and governed connectors with documented ownership and failure modes.
sub_criteria: Are AI systems integrated through APIs, service boundaries, events, or governed connectors rather than brittle point integrations?
Are legacy or brownfield systems wrapped or exposed through stable interfaces before AI agents depend on them?
Are integration ownership, versioning, dependencies, and failure modes documented?

criteria.title: AI Lifecycle & Release Control
criteria.description: Models, prompts, agents, tools, datasets, and evaluation suites are versioned and released through controlled lifecycle practices.
sub_criteria: Are models, prompts, agents, tools, datasets, configurations, and evaluation suites versioned?
Is there a controlled build-test-deploy-monitor-rollback lifecycle for AI-enabled services?
Can production behavior be traced back to model, prompt, data, tool, and release version?

criteria.title: AI Observability & Evaluation System
criteria.description: Production AI behavior is monitored through a Sense & Respond loop for quality, safety, cost, latency, groundedness, drift, and business impact.
sub_criteria: Are quality, safety, cost, latency, groundedness, drift, and business impact monitored in production?
Are offline and online evaluation methods defined for key AI use cases?
Do alerts, retraining triggers, intervention workflows, or service-owner reviews activate when AI performance, data freshness, value, or safety thresholds degrade?

criteria.title: Secure-by-Design AI Trust & Safety Layer
criteria.description: Trust and safety controls are embedded Secure-by-Design into AI workflows, including red teaming, guardrails, access controls, human escalation, and adversarial testing.
sub_criteria: Are prompt injection, data leakage, toxic content, unsafe tool use, and adversarial scenarios red-teamed before production?
Are guardrails, filters, access controls, and Human-in-the-Loop escalation paths embedded into AI workflows?
Is there an Agent Behavioral Contract defining what AI systems are forbidden to do, which tools they may use, and when they must escalate?

criteria.title: AI Platform as Product
criteria.description: Reusable AI platform products provide shared model access, data patterns, deployment templates, observability, evaluation, and developer experience.
sub_criteria: Are shared AI services, model gateways, data access patterns, MLOps/LLMOps capabilities, and deployment templates offered as internal platform products?
Are platform teams accountable to service-area teams as internal customers?
Are platform capabilities measured through adoption, flow, reliability, developer experience, and value enablement?

criteria.title: Purpose-Driven AI Strategy
criteria.description: AI ambition is connected to strategic purpose, customer value, business model choices, and explicit boundaries for where AI should not be used.
sub_criteria: Does the organization clearly define why AI matters to its strategy, customers, values, and business model?
Are AI ambition areas connected to service areas, value streams, or strategic domains?
Are where-not-to-use-AI boundaries explicitly defined?

criteria.title: Impact-Driven AI Value Framing
criteria.description: AI initiatives start from impact statements and value hypotheses, with evidence-based business cases, baseline and post-release measurement, and value metrics beyond cost reduction.
sub_criteria: Are AI initiatives started from explicit Impact Statements rather than tool ideas?
Are expected outcomes defined through customer value, profitability, ROCE/TVO, quality, first-time-right, flow, experience, or adaptability metrics?
Are value hypotheses tested and updated after pilots or production releases to support kill, continue, pivot, or scale decisions?

criteria.title: Embedded AI Governance Model
criteria.description: AI governance is embedded into ownership, architecture, security, data, service operations, and auditability as an enabling system.
sub_criteria: Are AI governance responsibilities embedded into service areas, platform teams, security, data, and business ownership?
Does governance enable safe value creation rather than only blocking risky initiatives?
Are exceptions, approvals, risks, and controls auditable?

criteria.title: Risk-Based Responsible AI Control
criteria.description: AI use cases are classified by risk and autonomy, with oversight, disclosure, logging, and accountability tied to risk level.
sub_criteria: Are AI use cases classified by risk, autonomy, user impact, data sensitivity, and regulatory exposure?
Are human oversight, escalation, disclosure, logging, and accountability requirements tied to risk level?
Are high-risk or autonomous scenarios blocked from production unless minimum controls are proven?

criteria.title: Evidence-Based AI Investment Portfolio
criteria.description: AI investment decisions use evidence about impact, risk, readiness, cost, and learning value to kill, continue, scale, or pivot.
sub_criteria: Are AI investments managed through portfolio logic using impact, risk, readiness, cost, and learning value?
Are kill, continue, scale, and pivot decisions based on evidence?
Does learning from pilots reprioritize the AI portfolio?

criteria.title: Domain-Owned AI Data Products
criteria.description: Critical AI data is owned by service areas or domains that understand meaning, quality, lifecycle, and usage expectations.
sub_criteria: Are critical AI datasets owned by the service area or business domain that understands the context?
Are data owners accountable for quality, meaning, lifecycle, and usability?
Are data products published with context, definitions, access rules, and usage expectations?

criteria.title: Context-Rich AI-Ready Data
criteria.description: Data carries semantic context, service meaning, process linkage, operational conditions, and decision relevance so AI systems can use it as contextual fuel.
sub_criteria: Does data include semantic context, source meaning, service/business process linkage, and operational conditions?
Can AI systems understand not only raw values but what those values mean in the service context?
Are critical data elements mapped to decisions, triggers, workflows, Jobs-to-Be-Done, or customer outcomes?

criteria.title: Data Quality & Lineage Control
criteria.description: AI-critical data is cataloged, versioned, quality-checked, freshness-monitored, readiness-level assessed, and traceable across training, retrieval, inference, and decisions.
sub_criteria: Are critical AI datasets cataloged, versioned, quality-checked, readiness-level assessed, and traceable?
Are freshness, completeness, correctness, and drift monitored?
Can training, retrieval, inference, and decision data be traced after the fact?

criteria.title: Governed AI Data Access
criteria.description: AI data access is role-based, auditable, purpose-limited, privacy-aware, and aligned with service or domain ownership.
sub_criteria: Are data classification, purpose limitation, access rights, and privacy controls documented?
Is access to AI data role-based, auditable, and aligned with service or domain ownership?
Are masking, anonymization, minimization, retention, and boundary controls used where required?

criteria.title: Reusable AI Data Access Patterns
criteria.description: Structured, unstructured, real-time, batch, feature, retrieval, embedding, and event-stream patterns are governed and reusable.
sub_criteria: Are structured, unstructured, real-time, batch, feature, and retrieval patterns defined for AI use?
Are RAG, embedding, search, feature-store, and event-stream patterns governed and reusable?
Is retrieval quality, source coverage, freshness, and grounding measured?

criteria.title: AI-Anchored Service & Capability Architecture
criteria.description: AI opportunities are mapped to service catalog, capabilities, customer paths, value streams, dependencies, platforms, data domains, and outcomes before solution design.
sub_criteria: Is there a current service catalog, business capability map, or equivalent model of value creation?
Are AI opportunities linked to services, capabilities, customer paths, value streams, or strategic service domains?
Are dependencies between capabilities, platforms, data, and service outcomes visible?

criteria.title: AI-Ready Service Blueprinting
criteria.description: Target services are blueprinted end-to-end so AI interventions improve the whole value stream, surface handoff risks, and avoid local task optimization.
sub_criteria: Are target services mapped end-to-end across customer journey, frontstage work, backstage work, systems, data, and handoffs?
Are bottlenecks, decision points, air gaps, failure modes, and automation candidates visible?
Are AI interventions placed where they improve the whole value stream, not only a local task?

criteria.title: Traceable AI Solution Structure
criteria.description: AI-enabled features are traceable from impact statement, customer need, and business outcome to capability, cognitive model, component, data, platform, risk, and work package.
sub_criteria: Are AI-enabled features decomposed into impact statement, business need, capability, cognitive model, component, data, platform, and work-package layers?
Can each AI use case be traced back to customer need, business outcome, and service architecture?
Are requirements, acceptance criteria, risks, and dependencies explicit before build?

criteria.title: Service Area Ownership of AI Value Creation
criteria.description: Integrated service-area teams own business, application, data, AI, and operational outcomes end to end.
sub_criteria: Are integrated service area teams accountable for business, application, data, and AI outcomes end-to-end?
Are platform teams positioned as enablers serving service-area teams?
Are AI solutions owned as living products within service areas rather than temporary projects?

criteria.title: Phased AI Scaling Through Service Areas
criteria.description: AI scales from Kickstart learning into Building-the-System rollout through service-area readiness, reusable patterns, platform capabilities, guardrails, feedback loops, and reassessment.
sub_criteria: Is scaling sequenced by service-area readiness, architectural clarity, data readiness, and risk level?
Are reusable patterns from pilots converted into playbooks, templates, platform capabilities, guardrails, and absorption-readiness evidence?
Is continuous improvement built into the rollout through Sense & Respond loops, retrospectives, readiness reassessment, and value realization review?
